opening: Is love still genuine when we have to work at giving it? And when we do something loving because we fear disappointing God, are we acting out of love or fear? Perhaps the answer lies in understanding what Christ is truly asking of us.
body:
Again, I find myself contemplating love. How difficult it can be to give, and how differently it seems to come to each of us. Some people have a natural generosity about them. They make room for others without a second thought, putting another person's needs before their own. I admire that kind of love because it seems to come from somewhere deep within them.

I see this in my husband. He has an extraordinary tenderness toward living creatures and often extends kindness to strangers without even thinking about it. When we're driving, he'll let another driver go first, even when he has the right of way. At the grocery store, he'll step aside and allow someone else to go ahead. Of course, he has his moments of anger and impatience, just as we all do. But there is something genuine about his generosity that I recognize and admire.

I would do almost anything for someone who needed me, yet I don't always find myself extending those same little kindnesses so naturally. I have to think about them. I have to make an effort. And lately, that has troubled me.

In today's first reading, from the Second Letter of John, we are told to love one another and to walk according to God's commandments. John also warns that whoever does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God.

Those words caught my attention because I have been questioning my own ability to love. I know how deeply I love God, Jesus, and the heavenly family. I know the extraordinary love He has made known to me. But I also know that I cannot always express that love toward others as freely as I would like.

And then fear enters.

What if I am not loving enough? What if I am not genuine? What if, when Christ returns, I am the one left behind?

Today's Gospel continues Jesus' teaching about the coming of the Son of Man. He speaks of the days of Noah and Lot, when people were eating, drinking, buying, selling, and carrying on with their lives. Then everything changed. Jesus warns His disciples to remain watchful and not become so attached to earthly life that they lose sight of God.

I read these words and think about how much of my own life is spent attending to ordinary responsibilities. There are finances to manage, bills to pay, decisions to make, and a future to prepare for. These things are necessary, but sometimes I wonder whether I have become so occupied with taking care of everything that I have forgotten how simply to love.

Yet I don't believe Jesus is telling us to abandon our responsibilities. Nor do I believe John is saying that only those who love effortlessly belong to God.

John tells us to walk in love. That word has stayed with me. Walking requires movement. It is something we continue doing, sometimes easily and sometimes with considerable effort.

Perhaps I have been confusing the natural expression of love with the genuineness of love itself.

There are people for whom small gestures of generosity seem instinctive. Others may express love through years of caregiving, sacrifice, responsibility, or quiet faithfulness. We cannot always see what is happening within another person's heart, nor can we measure our own love entirely by comparing ourselves with someone else.

But I also don't want to use that understanding as an excuse. I want to become more generous in the little moments. I want to notice the person who needs patience, kindness, or simply the opportunity to go ahead of me. I want God's love to emanate from me as naturally as I know it exists within Him.

And that brings me to the question that has been troubling me most.

Am I trying to love because I am afraid of losing God?

There is a difference between choosing love because we fear punishment and choosing love because we have come to know the One who first loved us.

In his First Letter, John writes, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear.”

I don't think this means we will never be afraid or struggle with loving others. But perhaps it means that fear is not where God wants our relationship with Him to remain.

I believe in a God whose love is everlasting, a love that does not disappear when our feelings change or when our human limitations become apparent. I believe that in His Kingdom we will finally know and give love without the fears and disappointments that accompany our earthly lives.

And yet Jesus has already told us that the Kingdom of God is among us.

So perhaps I need to stop asking whether I am loving enough to be welcomed into His Kingdom and begin asking how I can allow the love He has already given me to become more visible today.

Not to earn His love. Not to compete with someone else's goodness. Not because I am afraid of being left behind.

But because I love Him.

I may never express love in exactly the same way as my husband or anyone else. There will be moments when generosity comes easily and others when I must consciously choose it. But making that choice does not make the love false.

Perhaps genuine love is not always something that flows effortlessly from us. Sometimes it is something we must willingly give, even when our hearts are struggling.

And perhaps that is part of what it means to walk in Christ's commandments: to keep learning how to love, trusting that God is not waiting for us to fail, but inviting us to grow closer to Him.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  You know how deeply I love You, and You know the limitations of my heart. You see the times when love comes easily and the times when I struggle to give it.  Lord, I do not want to love others simply because I am afraid of disappointing You or being separated from You. I want to love because I know Your love, because I have received it, and because I want others to experience something of that same goodness.  Help me recognize the opportunities for kindness that I so easily overlook. Teach me patience, generosity, and tenderness, especially in the ordinary moments of my day.  When I compare myself with others, remind me that You know my heart. When fear enters my thoughts, help me trust in Your mercy without becoming complacent about the ways I still need to grow.  Jesus, let Your love become more natural within me. May I learn to give without fear, to serve without resentment, and to love without constantly questioning whether I have done enough.  And when I think of Your return, may I look toward that day with hope and longing rather than fear, trusting in Your mercy and continuing to walk in Your teachings.  Amen.
theme: Learning to give love freely, not because we fear losing God's love, but because we have already received it.
title: Let Love Rule
